SPIKE® LR2
5th Generation, Precision, Long-Range, EO-Guided Missile System for Ground, Air and Sea
________________

Powerful, Versatile, and Precise

SPIKE LR2 is a state-of-the-art, EO, multipurpose, multi-platform, 5th generation missile system that meets the complex needs of modern warfare.

The missile weapon system ‒ which can be used for infantry, armored vehicles, naval vessels and helicopters ‒ operates at long range, up to 5.5 km, with unparalleled precision. It successfully engages direct, non-line-of-sight, and beyond-line-of-sight targets.

SPIKE LR2 includes a powerful tandem HEAT warhead that can defeat any of today’s tanks, vehicles, or maritime vessels ‒ and can be used in urban combat against structural targets found in urban settings for in-structure detonation.

Benefits

Enhanced lethality against all types of targets; high hit probability
Range 5.5 km; pinpoint accuracy at long range
Multiple operational modes: Fire & Forget/Fire & Observe/Fire to Target Coordinates
Immune to GPS Jamming
Full commonality with all SPIKE missiles & launchers (ground, air, sea); interoperability with 34 user nations (19 in EU/NATO)
Reduced weight enables carrying two rounds by one soldier
Multipurpose/Multi-platform
Very low Life Cycle Cost (LCC)
Cutting-Edge Technologies

The SPIKE LR2 missile has an advanced high-end electro-optical seeker which includes a high-quality uncooled IR sensor and an advanced high-resolution day sensor. The system implements sensor data fusion via simultaneous operation of both VIS and IR sensors. This feature enables stronger and smarter tracking capabilities, even under the harshest weather conditions.

Unmatched Performance

The EO guidance system with real-time fiber-optic data link delivers multiple cutting-edge capabilities including man-in-the-loop retargeting, engagement of non-line-of-sight targets, and pinpoint precision. A novel multispectral tracker allows hot swapping (in-flight swapping IR/VIS channels), under the gunner’s control ‒ allowing the detection of hidden target IR signature as well as shape and color. Simple and easy to operate, the SPIKE LR2 system is immune to RF, GPS, or other jamming measures.

 

Optional Configurations

SPIKE LR2 can be supplied as a dismounted man portable system as well as a vehicle-mounted guided missile. Also available is a multipurpose missile configuration that includes gunner-controlled fusing for control of the desired effect, offering both breaching of bunkers with in-structure detonation upon breaching of up to 20cm of reinforced concrete (including steel reinforcing bars). It can also be used in air burst mode against combatants.

Main Capabilities

Embedded IMU for missions of 3rd party target allocation, network-enabled
Multispectral target tracker
Selectable flight trajectories offering low, medium or high angles of attack
Mid-flight abort-mission capability
Powerful warhead for increased lethality
Multipurpose configuration for breaching/peripheral blast

What does a "5th-generation" guided missile mean?
A 5th-generation guided missile combines advanced electro-optical sensing, multispectral target acquisition, real-time communication, multiple engagement modes, and enhanced battlefield flexibility. SPIKE LR2 integrates these capabilities with man-in-the-loop control, fiber-optic communication, multispectral IR/VIS sensing, GPS- and RF-jamming immunity, and precision engagement against both visible and concealed targets.

Is SPIKE LR2 an anti-tank guided missile (ATGM) or a multi-purpose missile?
SPIKE LR2 is both an advanced Anti-Tank Guided Missile (ATGM) and a multi-purpose precision-guided missile. While highly effective against modern armored vehicles, it is also designed to engage fortified structures, field fortifications, maritime targets, and other high-value objectives using different warhead configurations and operational modes.

What guidance modes does SPIKE LR2 support?
(Fire-and-Forget, Fire-and-Observe, Fire-to-Target Coordinates) SPIKE LR2 supports three primary guidance modes: Fire-and-Forget, Fire-and-Observe, and Fire-to-Target Coordinates. These modes provide operational flexibility for different mission scenarios, allowing autonomous engagement, real-time operator observation, or precision strikes against predefined coordinates. Combined with its fiber-optic data link and multispectral seeker, operators can maintain control, update engagements when required, and optimize mission effectiveness under changing battlefield conditions.

Is SPIKE LR2 immune to GPS and RF jamming?
Yes. SPIKE LR2 is designed to operate in contested electromagnetic environments and is immune to GPS and RF jamming. Its advanced electro-optical seeker, multispectral sensors, and fiber-optic communication link allow the missile to maintain accurate target tracking and engagement without relying on GPS signals or vulnerable radio-frequency guidance. Instead, guidance is primarily based on electro-optical tracking and fiber-optic communication, ensuring reliable performance even in GPS- and RF-denied environments.

What warhead options does SPIKE LR2 offer?
(Tandem HEAT, Multipurpose, In-Structure Detonation) SPIKE LR2 offers multiple warhead configurations to support diverse mission requirements. The Tandem HEAT warhead is optimized for defeating modern main battle tanks and armored vehicles, while the Multipurpose warhead supports engagement of structures, fortified positions, and other battlefield targets. The missile also supports in-structure detonation and configurable effects, enabling operators to match the warhead to different operational scenarios.

Ізраїль замовив 12 ударних гелікоптерів Apache

Міністерство оборони Ізраїлю підписало угоду з США про закупівлю 12 ударних гелікоптерів AH-64E Apache виробництва американської компанії Boeing.

Про підписання контракту повідомили у Міністерстві оборони Ізраїлю та виданні The Times of Israel.

Фінансування угоди у розмірі близько $280 мільйонів було затверджене урядом після декількох перенесень дедлайнів, встановлених американською стороною.

Для покриття витрат уряд Ізраїлю перерозподілив бюджетні кошти, урізавши фінансування з п’ятирічної програми інвестицій у соціальний та економічний розвиток арабського сектору.

Міністр фінансів Бецалель Смотрич назвав закупівлю помилкою, заявивши, що роль гелікоптерів можуть виконувати безпілотники, однак прем’єр-міністр Беньямін Нетаньягу наполіг на підписанні угоди.

Ударний гелікоптер AH-64D Повітряних сил Ізраїлю. Фото: Міністерство оборони Ізраїлю

Постачання гелікоптерів для Повітряних сил Ізраїлю за підписаним контрактом розпочнеться на початку 2030-х років.

Ізраїль отримає гелікоптери у найсучаснішій модифікації AH-64E, яка вирізняється підвищеною потужністю двигунів, оновленою авіонікою та можливістю керувати безпілотниками з кабіни.

Наразі на озброєнні Ізраїлю перебуває близько 40–48 ударних гелікоптерів Apache двох модифікацій — AH-64A Peten та більш сучасної AH-64D Saraf.

Загалом ізраїльський арсенал розподілений між двома основними ескадрильями, проте через інтенсивну експлуатацію впродовж тривалого часу та високе навантаження під час останніх бойових дій парк потребує відновлення й оновлення.

Гелікоптер AH-64E Apache запускає дрон Altius 700. Березень 2026. Джерело: Anduril

Ударний гелікоптер AH-64E Apache призначений для знищення бронетехніки, живої сили, а також для вогневої підтримки сухопутних підрозділів на полі бою.

Основним озброєнням гелікоптера є 30-мм автоматична гармата M230 з боєкомплектом до 1200 снарядів, а також керовані протитанкові ракети AGM-114 Hellfire та 70-мм некеровані або високоточні ракети APKWS.

Модифікація AH-64E оснащена двома двигунами General Electric T700-GE-701D потужністю понад 1990 к.с. кожен, що забезпечує максимальну швидкість польоту до 300 км/год та практичну стелю понад 6000 метрів.

The Interceptor Bubble

Russia is three steps ahead. Are the people writing the checks asking why?

Those of us that study conflict knows that Russia is currently preparing a winter campaign against Ukraine’s energy grid. Every winter since the beginning of the conflict, it strikes power stations, substations and the heating plants that keep apartment blocks habitable when the temperature falls below freezing. This year, Ukrainian intelligence reports that Moscow has prioritized production of its newest jet-powered Geran drones to build stockpiles for that campaign. The weapon that will test Ukraine’s air defenses this winter is not the weapon Western investors have paid out, and many EU governments have used tax payer money in contract awards to defeat.

That gap between the threat that was funded and the threat that is arriving is the subject of this article. It is a question sia’s licensed and then domestically produced copy of Iran’s Shahed-136. It flew at tic sensor networks to hear it coming, mobile fire teams with heavy machine guns mounted on pickup trucks, German-made Gepard and Skynex gun systems for point defense, electronic warfare (EW) to jam its satellite navigation, and, over time, cheap interceptor drones that could climb, chase and ram it. By some accounts, Ukraine’s interception rate against the propeller-driven Gerans approached 90 percent.

That success became a business plan. Founders in the United States, Britain and Western Europe went to venture investors with a simple proposition: the Shahed is the defining aerial threat of modern war, and we will build the low-cost interceptor that defeats it at scale. The proposition was sound in 2024. The money arrived in 2025 and 2026, and it arrived in volume. Defense technology startups drew $19.8 billion in venture funding in the first quarter of 2026 alone, against $5.7 billion in the first quarter of 2024. European defense technology is on track for a record year of more than $10 billion. Early-stage companies in the sector have been priced at 17 to 50 times revenue. Several interceptor firms have raised hundreds of millions of dollars and carry valuations in the billions, some less than two years after incorporation. Contracts from the US Department of Defense (DoD) and the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) followed, and those contracts were then cited to justify the next round at a higher price.

The difficulty is that Russia read the same battlefield data, drew its own conclusions, and moved first.

Three steps ahead

The Russian response to Ukraine’s counter-drone success has been methodical, and it has been fast. Consider the sequence.

Step one was to harden the navigation. The original Iranian design carried a satellite navigation receiver with a four-element antenna. Ukrainian jamming exploited that weakness. Russia responded with controlled reception pattern antennas (CRPA), arrays that electronically steer their sensitivity away from a jammer. By January 2025, Russian drones carried Chinese-sourced modules with 16 antenna elements. By the end of 2025, Gerans built at the Izhevsk plant flew with the Kometa-M16, a 16-element array in three rows. Analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) called it unprecedented wartime iteration. In one documented case, a satellite receiver installed in early October 2025 was on the battlefield within a week.

Step two was to connect the drones. Russian engineers added 3G and LTE (Long-Term Evolution, the 4G cellular standard) modems as early as late 2023, then standardized telemetry modules built around off-the-shelf minicomputers. By the summer of 2025, Chinese mesh radio modems allowed Gerans to relay signals through one another, giving operators real-time control and the ability to reroute a drone in flight. On Sept. 25 of this year, during a strike on a business centre in Kyiv, one jet drone circled the target at almost three kilometres of altitude as a relay, passing control signals to the Geran-5 that hit the building while filming the attack.

Step three was speed and altitude. In 2025, the Geran-3 introduced a jet engine and raised cruise speed to roughly 330 kilometres per hour. In August 2026, Russia halted Geran-3 production and moved to the Geran-4, with a top speed near 500 kilometres per hour, and the Geran-5, a cruise-missile-like airframe powered by a Chinese Telefly turbojet. According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Geran-5 cruises at 450 to 600 kilometres per hour, sia’s Kh-101 cruise missile. Ukrainian intelligence has not confirmed the designation, but a Russian military correspondent has referred to an autonomous optical navigation system named “Susanin” on the Geran series. A drone that can navigate by looking at the terrain does not need satellites, and a drone that does not need satellites cannot be jammed off course. Gerans now carry long-wave infrared (LWIR) cameras paired with laser rangefinders. Russia has fitted some with R-60 air-to-air missiles and Verba shoulder-fired missiles to threaten the helicopters and aircraft that hunt them, and by March 2026 some carried two first-person view (FPV) drones for release in mid-flight. The Geran has become a family of weapons, launched in mixed salvos alongside Gerbera decoys designed to soak up interceptors.

The scale matters as much as the design. In June, Russia launched roughly 450 jet-powered Gerans. In August, it launched more than 2,800. In some attacks, more than 70 percent of the drones are now jet variants. Ukraine’s interception rate against them has fallen to e the strengths and failures are instructive.

Electronic warfare.

EW was once the cheapest and most effective layer. Jamming costs almost nothing per engagement and can affect many drones at once. Against the CRPA arrays, mesh networking, Starlink connectivity and optical navigation now in Russian service, it has lost much of that advantage. EW still has a role in degrading datalinks and confusing sensors, but no serious analyst now treats it as the primary kill mechanism against a modern Geran. Any company whose core value is a jammer pitched against long-range attack drones should be asked what it does against a target that no longer relies on the signals it jams.

Guns.

The Gepard and Skynex systems have been among the stars of Ukraine’s air defense. A burst costs in the region of $5,000, and at close range they are reliable. Their limitation is reach. They are last-layer point defenses with effective ranges measured in a few kilometers. A Geran-5 transiting at five kilometers of altitude and 600 kilometers per hour crosses a gun’s engagement envelope in seconds, if it enters it at all. The mobile fire teams with machine guns that did so much damage to the Geran-2 are of little use against a target flying several kilometers above them at three times the speed.

Interceptor drones.

This is where the most money has gone and where the most important lessons sit. Ukrainian interceptors cost $1,000 to $3,000 each. One Ukrainian maker, General Cherry, reported 3,296 kills with its Bullet interceptor in February alone. The American-designed Merops system, which emerged from a US-backed effort with links to former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt, costs ing their products. If they have struggled, Western products designed far from the front deserve harder scrutiny than they are receiving.

Rockets and low-cost kinetics.

Laser-guided rockets such as the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) cost $15,000 to $20,000 per round and were validated against drones in April 2026, but they are launched from aircraft, which brings the cost and limits of the aircraft with them. KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries.

Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month. They can now reach speeds of up to 373 mph (600 km/h) — more than three times the speed of the propeller-driven Geran-2 drones they evolved from — far exceeding the top velocity of the average Ukrainian interceptor drone, air force officials told lawmakers last week.

To stop the drones, Ukraine must instead rely on F-16s, newly installed machine gun turrets that use artificial intelligence to aim and costly air-defense missiles that are in short supply globally.

“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector. But Russia did not listen to the American president,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after jets seriously damaged a gas production facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday night.

Russia launched 167 missiles and drones overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, including 77 jet-powered drones, which officials said struck one of Kyiv’s main power plants and left 600,000 without power.

Ukraine’s Air Force says they are beginning to field more effective countermeasures, but with Russia continuing to optimize the design of jet-powered drones to destroy critical infrastructure, the development of jets and anti-jet interceptors has become the latest neck-and-neck technology race on the battlefield.

Iran shipped Russia its first Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 drones in mid-August 2022, and Moscow rebranded them the Geran-1 and Geran-2 and was firing them at Ukrainian civilian infrastructure by that October.

Those propeller-driven drones were slow enough for Ukraine to build an economical defense around mobile fire teams and cheap interceptor drones rather than spending scarce missiles on every Shahed, and in February the interceptors accounted for more than 70% of Shahed downings over Kyiv.

The jet-powered Gerans are outrunning that defense, and Russia has since stopped building the slower Geran-3 and ramped up production of the Geran-4, which cruises at 217 to 311 mph (350 to 500 km/h), and the missile-shaped Geran-5, which carries a 90-kilogram (198-pound) warhead, Militarnyi reported in August, citing Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, known as HUR.

“The Geran-5 flies 150km/h faster than the Geran-4, so the goal is to intercept from the front rather than the rear — a much harder problem to solve,” an engineer at a Ukrainian defense contractor told the Kyiv Independent.

And they are still getting faster, with the Air Force projecting speeds of 500 to 560 mph (800 to 900 km/h), though none have been recorded yet, its deputy commander, Col. Yurii Cherevashenko, told a parliamentary commission Oct. 6.

A Geran-4 version Russia began flying this autumn is built to take out infrastructure, navigating by a U.S.-made magnetometer and an optical system and carrying a new warhead designed to cut bridges and power line supports, HUR said in an Oct. 5 statement.

The new 88-pound (40-kilogram) warhead “was created specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and iron bridge structures,” Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an EW expert and adviser to Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram Sept. 30 when Russia was first spotted using the upgrade on a jet drone.

These optimized Russian jet drones hit Kyiv’s South Bridge, which carries cars and metro trains across the Dnipro River, at least five times on Oct. 1 and 2, once exploding near a pier as a train crossed overhead, then struck the city’s North Bridge on Oct. 3, officials said.

Ukrainian interceptors stopped roughly 90% of the older propeller-driven drones, but against the jets, the interception rate has been significantly lower.

“Initially, we saw a very low interception rate in Ukraine. It then rose to more than 30%, and in recent nights it has increased to over 50%,” Matthias Lehna, vice president of German drone maker Quantum Systems, told Ukrinform last week.

Air force officials reported downing 77% of incoming jet-powered drones on Tuesday night.

Ukraine put its first jet interceptor, the Alexa Spatium, into service only on Aug. 21, and a handful of other prototypes, including Wild Hornets’ STING S and SkyFall’s P1-SUN Jetkiller, have successfully downed a small number of Geran-5s, according to officials speaking to the Kyiv Independent.

Fourteen companies are flight-testing jet interceptors with the Air Force, and three have shown promising results, but the deputy air force commander said officials don’t expect the jet interceptors to be delivered at the scale Ukraine needs until the end of November at the earliest.

“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector. But Russia did not listen to the American president,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after jets seriously damaged a gas production facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday night.

Russia launched 167 missiles and drones overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, including 77 jet-powered drones, which officials said struck one of Kyiv’s main power plants and left 600,000 without power.

Ukraine’s Air Force says they are beginning to field more effective countermeasures, but with Russia continuing to optimize the design of jet-powered drones to destroy critical infrastructure, the development of jets and anti-jet interceptors has become the latest neck-and-neck technology race on the battlefield.

Iran shipped Russia its first Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 drones in mid-August 2022, and Moscow rebranded them the Geran-1 and Geran-2 and was firing them at Ukrainian civilian infrastructure by that October.

Those propeller-driven drones were slow enough for Ukraine to build an economical defense around mobile fire teams and cheap interceptor drones rather than spending scarce missiles on every Shahed, and in February the interceptors accounted for more than 70% of Shahed downings over Kyiv.

The jet-powered Gerans are outrunning that defense, and Russia has since stopped building the slower Geran-3 and ramped up production of the Geran-4, which cruises at 217 to 311 mph (350 to 500 km/h), and the missile-shaped Geran-5, which carries a 90-kilogram (198-pound) warhead, Militarnyi reported in August, citing Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, known as HUR.

A Geran-4 version Russia began flying this autumn is built to take out infrastructure, navigating by a U.S.-made magnetometer and an optical system and carrying a new warhead designed to cut bridges and power line supports, HUR said in an Oct. 5 statement.

Fourteen companies are flight-testing jet interceptors with the Air Force, and three have shown promising results, but the deputy air force commander said officials don’t expect the jet interceptors to be delivered at the scale Ukraine needs until the end of November at the earliest.

Jet drones already make up approximately 40% of the drones Russia launches and the Air Force expects that share to reach up to 80% of total attacks.

U.S. Navy gives Boeing up to $80M to improve MQ-25 drone

MQ-25A Stingray uncrewed tanker

Photo by Boeing Defense

Key Points

The U.S. Navy has given Boeing a contract worth up to $80 million to keep developing and improving the MQ-25A Stingray, the uncrewed tanker designed to refuel fighter jets from aircraft carrier decks.

The indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, announced by the U.S. Department of War, covers system improvements, development and integration of new aircraft configurations, production readiness and sustainment work for the MQ-25A. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, awarded it on a sole-source basis, with work to be done in St. Louis, Missouri, through October 2031. No money was obligated at signing; the U.S. Navy will fund the work through individual orders as it needs them.

The MQ-25A is the U.S. Navy’s first operational carrier-based drone. Its main job is aerial refueling, a task now often handled by F/A-18E/F Super Hornets carrying fuel tanks, which takes fighters away from combat missions. Handing that work to an uncrewed tanker is meant to free up Super Hornets and extend how far the carrier air wing can strike.

- 
The new contract follows a busy year for the program. The first production-representative MQ-25A flew for ly while U.S. Navy operators sent commands from a ground control station, Boeing said. On May 19, the U.S. Navy granted the program Milestone C approval, clearing it to enter low-rate initial production.

As part of that decision, the U.S. Navy said it expected a first low-rate production contract for three aircraft, with priced options for three more in a second lot and five in a third, Breaking Defense reported. The program of record calls for 76 aircraft, including four engineering development models and five system demonstration test articles, according to USNI News.

The Stingray has a long development history. Boeing’s T1 test aircraft first flew in September 2019, and in June 2021 it became the first uncrewed aircraft to refuel another aircraft in flight when it passed fuel to a Super Hornet. The program later slipped by several years: initial operational capability, defined as three MQ-25As with trained personnel ready to deploy on a carrier, was first planned for 2024 and is now expected in fiscal 2029.

Ships are being prepared alongside the aircraft. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) became the first fully operational carrier able to handle the MQ-25 in 2026, after the U.S. Navy installed its first Unmanned Carrier Aviation Mission Control System aboard USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) in 2024, according to the Congressional Research Service.

Orders under the new $80 million contract will run through October 2031, as the MQ-25A moves through flight testing and toward carrier deployment.

Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid

KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries.

Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month. They can now reach speeds of up to 373 mph (600 km/h) — more than three times the speed of the propeller-driven Geran-2 drones they evolved from — far exceeding the top velocity of the average Ukrainian interceptor drone, air force officials told lawmakers last week.

To stop the drones, Ukraine must instead rely on F-16s, newly installed machine gun turrets that use artificial intelligence to aim and costly air-defense missiles that are in short supply globally.

“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector. But Russia did not listen to the American president,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after jets seriously damaged a gas production facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday night.

Russia launched 167 missiles and drones overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, including 77 jet-powered drones, which officials said struck one of Kyiv’s main power plants and left 600,000 without power.

Ukraine’s Air Force says they are beginning to field more effective countermeasures, but with Russia continuing to optimize the design of jet-powered drones to destroy critical infrastructure, the development of jets and anti-jet interceptors has become the latest neck-and-neck technology race on the battlefield.

Iran shipped Russia its first Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 drones in mid-August 2022, and Moscow rebranded them the Geran-1 and Geran-2 and was firing them at Ukrainian civilian infrastructure by that October.

Those propeller-driven drones were slow enough for Ukraine to build an economical defense around mobile fire teams and cheap interceptor drones rather than spending scarce missiles on every Shahed, and in February the interceptors accounted for more than 70% of Shahed downings over Kyiv.

The jet-powered Gerans are outrunning that defense, and Russia has since stopped building the slower Geran-3 and ramped up production of the Geran-4, which cruises at 217 to 311 mph (350 to 500 km/h), and the missile-shaped Geran-5, which carries a 90-kilogram (198-pound) warhead, Militarnyi reported in August, citing Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, known as HUR.

“The Geran-5 flies 150km/h faster than the Geran-4, so the goal is to intercept from the front rather than the rear — a much harder problem to solve,” an engineer at a Ukrainian defense contractor told the Kyiv Independent.

And they are still getting faster, with the Air Force projecting speeds of 500 to 560 mph (800 to 900 km/h), though none have been recorded yet, its deputy commander, Col. Yurii Cherevashenko, told a parliamentary commission Oct. 6.

A Geran-4 version Russia began flying this autumn is built to take out infrastructure, navigating by a U.S.-made magnetometer and an optical system and carrying a new warhead designed to cut bridges and power line supports, HUR said in an Oct. 5 statement.

The new 88-pound (40-kilogram) warhead “was created specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and iron bridge structures,” Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an EW expert and adviser to Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram Sept. 30 when Russia was first spotted using the upgrade on a jet drone.

These optimized Russian jet drones hit Kyiv’s South Bridge, which carries cars and metro trains across the Dnipro River, at least five times on Oct. 1 and 2, once exploding near a pier as a train crossed overhead, then struck the city’s North Bridge on Oct. 3, officials said.

Ukrainian interceptors stopped roughly 90% of the older propeller-driven drones, but against the jets, the interception rate has been significantly lower.

“Initially, we saw a very low interception rate in Ukraine. It then rose to more than 30%, and in recent nights it has increased to over 50%,” Matthias Lehna, vice president of German drone maker Quantum Systems, told Ukrinform last week.

Air force officials reported downing 77% of incoming jet-powered drones on Tuesday night.

Ukraine put its first jet interceptor, the Alexa Spatium, into service only on Aug. 21, and a handful of other prototypes, including Wild Hornets’ STING S and SkyFall’s P1-SUN Jetkiller, have successfully downed a small number of Geran-5s, according to officials speaking to the Kyiv Independent.

Fourteen companies are flight-testing jet interceptors with the Air Force, and three have shown promising results, but the deputy air force commander said officials don’t expect the jet interceptors to be delivered at the scale Ukraine needs until the end of November at the earliest.

Jet drones already make up approximately 40% of the drones Russia launches and the Air Force expects that share to reach up to 80% of total attacks.

Україна використала британські безекіпажні надводні катери K3 Scout під час атаки на російське судно в порту Сочі.

Про це повідомляє видання The Times із посиланням на джерела в оборонній промисловості.

За даними видання, 3 вересня щонайменше два безекіпажні апарати увійшли до порту Сочі та атакували російське судно Nefrit.

Один із дронів подолав оборонний периметр і пошкодив лівий борт судна. Другий не дістався цілі та вибухнув.

За даними The Times, для атаки використали катери K3 Scout виробництва британської компанії Kraken Technology.

Галузеві джерела підтвердили The Times, що компанія поставила ці апарати для використання щонайменше під час одного бойового удару по російському судну.

Морський безпілотник, помічений очевидцями під час удару в Сочі, 3 вересня 2026 року. Кадр з відео ЗМІ РФ

K3 Scout — це безекіпажний надводний катер завдовжки близько 8,5 метра.

Максимальна швидкість апарата становить приблизно 55 вузлів, або 102 км/год, а корисне навантаження може сягати 600 кг. Такі характеристики дають змогу використовувати його для ударних місій.

Крім того, катер можна обладнати для транспортування FPV-дронів.

Заявлена дальність ходу K3 Scout становить близько 650 морських миль, або 1200 км. Цього показника достатньо для подолання відстані від Одеси до Сочі.

Водночас компанія випробовує й альтернативні способи доставки катерів до віддалених районів.

CHAOS Industries unveils VESPID counter-drone interceptors with 10-kilometer range and annual production target of 12,000 units

CHAOS Industries has unveiled VESPID, a family of autonomous counter-drone interceptors that it plans to manufacture at an initial rate of 12,000 a year. The Los Angeles-based company says the design can cut costs by up to 90% compared with conventional solid-rocket-motor and turbojet interceptors.

The family includes the man-portable Mk 0 and the faster, more maneuverable Mk 1 for multitube launchers. Both are designed to defend against Group 1–3 unmanned aircraft and one-way attack threats.

VESPID uses an electric ducted fan and commercial off-the-shelf drone electronics. CHAOS says the interceptor weighs less than 12 pounds, launches in under five seconds and can engage targets up to 10 kilometers away in under 100 seconds.

Thrust vector control enables maneuvering against targets attempting to evade interception. The weapon destroys its target through direct impact rather than an explosive warhead.

“The United States and its allies require more than expensive, exquisite systems that take years to develop and are produced in limited quantities,” said Dr. Bo Marr, co-founder and chief technology officer of CHAOS Industries. “We need effective interceptors that can be built quickly, fielded broadly, and employed at a cost that makes sense against threats arriving at scale.”

CHAOS has not disclosed a unit price. Its manufacturing architecture is designed to support expansion to 50,000 interceptors annually as customer demand grows.

During the midcourse phase, VESPID receives guidance from CHAOS radars or an external command-and-control system. A direct-to-radar datalink narrows the area the terminal seeker must search and, according to the company, improves resistance to jamming.

The interceptor then switches to a commercial long-wave infrared seeker with AI-enabled target acquisition and guidance. CHAOS says engagement requires no operator input after launch and does not depend on GPS.

VESPID can integrate with existing sensors, command systems and launch platforms. Its connection to CHAOS’ NEXUS command-and-control system is intended to coordinate responses to drone swarms.

The family is interoperable with CHAOS’ multistatic radars, including VANQUISH PRIME systems. When paired with a CHAOS radar, the interceptor’s datalink signal also helps NEXUS distinguish it from hostile aircraft.

The Mk 0 can be assembled in under a minute without special tools. It launches vertically under electric fan power from the ground or a truck bed, with its battery and wings removed for transport.

The Mk 1 uses a tubular launcher with a pyrotechnic launch cartridge. CHAOS says a 10-round trainable launcher is available and gives an engagement velocity of 150 meters per second, or more than 300 miles per hour.

A planned version would carry more than 100 interceptors in a 20-foot ISO container. That configuration is intended for integration with uncrewed ground or surface vehicles.

CHAOS is relying on commercial components and simplified assembly to support high-volume production. The company’s stated aim is to give forces enough affordable interceptors to sustain protection against repeated drone attacks.

“Affordability and the ability to rapidly replace capability are not secondary considerations,” Marr said. “They are operational advantages.”

The company announced VESPID on October 12 and scheduled the Mk 1’s first public display aboard a Forterra MESA vehicle at AUSA 2026 in Washington. Founded in 2022, CHAOS manufactures its systems in the United States and has raised $1 billion from investors including 8VC, Accel and Valor Equity Partners.

TENCORE представила екосистему наземних роботизованих комплексів

Українська компанія TENCORE оголосила про запуск TENCORE ECOSYSTEM — екосистеми наземних роботизованих комплексів, яка об’єднує чотири класи платформ для військових і цивільних завдань.

Про це компанія повідомила Мілітарному.

У компанії називають її першою в Україні цілісною екосистемою такого типу. Вона має охоплювати широкий спектр завдань — від логістики, евакуації та вогневої підтримки до подолання водних перешкод і пожежно-рятувальних робіт.

За задумом розробника, об’єднання різних платформ в одну систему має спростити їхнє застосування, обслуговування та інтеграцію додаткового обладнання.

У TENCORE зазначають, що використання великої кількості різнотипних наземних роботизованих комплексів створює додаткові проблеми з логістикою, навчанням екіпажів, ремонтом і сумісністю засобів зв’язку.

Дрон TerMIT 2.0. Джерело: компанія Tencore

Основу TENCORE ECOSYSTEM становлять чотири наземні роботизовані платформи різного призначення.

Перша — гусеничний TerMIT, побудований за модульною схемою. Залежно від установленого обладнання комплекс може виконувати логістичні та інженерні завдання, евакуювати поранених або використовуватися як носій бойових модулів.

TerMIT уже серійно використовується українськими військовими — у липні TENCORE безоплатно передала Силам оборони ще 29 таких комплексів для логістики, евакуації та ударних місій.

У серпні компанія випробовувала для TerMIT 2.0 бойовий модуль із реактивними вогнеметами РПВ-16. Окремо для машини створили модуль евакуації пошкоджених або застряглих НРК.

Другий елемент екосистеми — колісний TOR 4×4. Він отримав броньовані колеса Run-Flat і орієнтований передусім на логістику та перевезення вантажів у складних умовах.

Третя платформа — амфібійний колісний всюдихід MAT1LDA 8×8, розроблений компанією NODRICS. Його призначенням є рух складними ґрунтами та форсування водних перешкод.

Четвертим елементом стала гусенична TRAX UTILITY — dual-use платформа для пожежно-рятувальних робіт, яку планують використовувати як у цивільному секторі, так і у спеціалізованих підрозділах.

TRAX Utility оснащена дистанційно керованим лафетним стволом із регульованою подачею води від 300 до 2000 літрів на хвилину. Дальність дистанційного керування заявлена до 3 км. За даними компанії, прототип уже залучали до ліквідації наслідків російських ударів у Київській області.

Зображення модуля AI KIT. Джерело: Tencore.

Окремим елементом нової екосистеми має стати уніфіковане додаткове обладнання. Одним із перших таких рішень є AI KIT — програмно-апаратний модуль, який дозволяє наземному комплексу продовжувати рух за маршрутом або повертатися після втрати зв’язку з оператором.

Про розробку цієї системи розповідав у травні Мілітарному CEO та співзасновник компанії Tencore Максим Васильченко, коли компанія тестувала автопілот для роботи НРК без стабільного GPS і зв’язку.

У липні TENCORE офіційно представила функціонал AI KIT, зокрема, алгоритм автоматичного повернення машини після повної втрати сигналу.

TENCORE також планує відкрити екосистему для інших українських та іноземних Defense Tech компаній. За задумом, сторонні розробники зможуть інтегрувати власні модулі й технології на серійні платформи компанії. Заявлена виробнича спроможність становить понад 500 наземних платформ на місяць.

У червні німецька Quantum Systems та TENCORE створили спільне підприємство Quantum Tencore Industries для виробництва TerMIT у Німеччині. Перший контракт передбачає виготовлення 2000 наземних роботизованих комплексів протягом 12 місяців для Сил оборони України.

Як зазначає компанія, від початку повномасштабного вторгнення TENCORE поставила Силам оборони понад 4000 роботизованих платформ, які використовуються більш ніж у 50 бригадах.

Злітна маса апарата становить 13,5 кг, із них маса бойової частини — 5 кг. Довжина фюзеляжу — 1,6 м, розмах крил — 1,9 м, заявлена швидкість польоту — 108–300 км/год, максимальна висота — 2 км.

«Сюрприз» — ударний квадрокоптер компанії «Робоавиа», який розробили для Сухопутних військ РФ. Він призначений для ураження наземних цілей скиданням боєприпасів. Конструкція складається, що дозволяє переносити апарат у рюкзаку. Заявлено, що маса квадрокоптера становить 24 кг, а максимальне корисне навантаження — 7 кг. Як варіант озброєння заявлені дві 82-мм мінометні міни.

На Ростовщині уразили підприємство, яке виготовляє дрони камікадзе «Клин»

Сили оборони уразили виробничо-складську будівлю підприємства «Робоавиа», яке виготовляє дрони камікадзе «Клин» оснащені ШІ, поблизу населеного пункту хутор Леніна Ростовської області РФ.

Про це повідомила пресслужба Генерального штабу Збройних Сил України.

За інформацією відомства, унаслідок удару 16 жовтня пошкоджень зазнала інфраструктура підприємства. Компанія також виготовляє розвідувальні безпілотники «Сарыч-2» та квадрокоптери «Сюрприз».

За інформацією «Центру журналістських розслідувань», компанія наразі має чотири виробничі та одну навчальну локацію в окупованому Криму й Росії. За інформацією розслідувачів, у 2023–2025 роках дохід ТОВ «Робоавиа» зріс із 450 млн до 1,7 млрд рублів, а чистий прибуток за 2025 рік збільшився вп’ятеро.

У 2015 році компанія розпочала роботу на базі авіаклубу на вул. Данилова, 62А в окупованому Сімферополі й продовжує працювати там донині. За цією адресою в базах даних значаться відділ програмного забезпечення та служба безпеки сімферопольського підрозділу ТОВ «Робоавиа».

Друга сімферопольська виробнича локація «Робоавиа» розміщена за адресою: вулиця Крилова, 133. За даними ЦЖР, у приміщеннях колишньої швейної фабрики УТОГ розташовані цех полімерних і композитних виробів та кілька дільниць: механічної обробки, електроніки, збирання й комплектації літальних апаратів, їхнього налаштування та випробування, цільових навантажень.

У грудні 2023 року компанія «Робоавиа» змінила юридичну адресу із Сімферополя на Ростовську область, Аксайський район, хутір Леніна, вул. Степова, будівля 1, споруда 1. У 2024 році повідомлялось, що компанія інвестує понад 752 млн рублів (близько 8 млн доларів за середнім курсом 2024 року) у створення виробництва БпЛА в Аксайському районі Ростовської області.

За даними з відкритих джерел, у виробничих спорудах на хуторі Леніна можуть працювати близько 40 співробітників. До штату цього підрозділу входять генеральний директор компанії, його заступник із безпеки, головні та провідні інженери, технологи, електроніки й енергетики.

Найбільший виробничий підрозділ «Робоавиа» розміщений у Ростові-на-Дону, на вул. Червоноармійській, 9. За цією адресою ще з 1960-х років діє оборонно-космічне підприємство, наразі відоме під назвою АТ «Виробничо-конструкторське підприємство «ИРИС»», що підпорядковане Роскосмосу.

«Сарыч-2» — розвідувальний безпілотник компанії «Робоавиа», призначений для повітряного спостереження та виявлення цілей. Апарат виконаний за схемою «літаюче крило» й оснащений електродвигуном. За повідомленнями 2023 року, він пройшов апробацію на Чорноморському флоті РФ. Заявлена злітна маса безпілотника становить 14 кг, розмах крила — 3,1 м.
